notes.text: I perceive of a truth — More clearly than ever, from such a concurrence of circumstances. That God is not a respecter of persons - Is not partial in his love. The words mean, in a particular sense, that he does not confine his love to one nation; in a general, that he is loving to every man, and willeth all men should be saved.

But in every nation he that feareth God and worketh righteousness — He that, first, reverences God, as great, wise, good, the cause, end, and governor of all things; and secondly, from this awful regard to him, not only avoids all known evil, but endeavours, according to the best light he has, to do all things well; is accepted of him - Through Christ, though he knows him not. The assertion is express, and admits of no exception. He is in the favour of God, whether enjoying his written word and ordinances or not. Nevertheless the addition of these is an unspeakable blessing to those who were before in some measure accepted. Otherwise God would never have sent an angel from heaven to direct Cornelius to St. Peter.

This is the word which God sent — When he sent his Son into the world, preaching - Proclaiming by him-peace between God and man, whether Jew or Gentile, by the God-man. He is Lord of both; yea, Lord of and over all.

Ye know the word which was published — You know the facts in general, the meaning of which I shall now more particularly explain and confirm to you. The baptism which John preached - To which he invited them by his preaching, in token of their repentance. This began in Galilee, which is near Cesarea.

How God anointed Jesus — Particularly at his baptism, thereby inaugurating him to his office: with the Holy Ghost and with power - It is worthy our remark, that frequently when the Holy Ghost is mentioned there is added a word particularly adapted to the present circumstance. So the deacons were to be full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, chap. vi, 3. Barnabas was full of the Holy Ghost and faith, chap. xi, 24. The disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost, chap. xiii, 52. And here, where his mighty works are mentioned, Christ himself is said to be anointed with the Holy Ghost and with power. For God was with him-He speaks sparingly here of the majesty of Christ, as considering the state of his hearers.
Not now to all the people — As before his death; to us who did eat and drink with him - That is, conversed familiarly and continually with him, in the time of his ministry.

It is he who is ordained by God the Judge of the living and the dead — Of all men, whether they are alive at his coming, or had died before it. This was declaring to them, in the strongest terms, how entirely their happiness depended on a timely and humble subjection to him who was to be their final Judge.

To him give all the prophets witness — Speaking to heathens he does not quote any in particular; that every one who believeth in him - Whether he be Jew or Gentile; receiveth remission of sins - Though he had not before either feared God, or worked righteousness.

glossa.text: *He is not a respecter of persons,* etc. ((BEDA.)) It is plain that God is not a respecter of persons, etc., *as far as* but that they should receive all that believe.

*You know,* etc. ((RAB.)) It is to be read thus: You know Jesus as John preached him: Jesus of Nazareth, how he anointed him, etc. Or: this John preached, that he anointed him, not indeed after an earthly manner, but by the spirit and the power of signs.

*Who went about,* etc. In the Greek is added, *through forty days,* not that they ate and drank with him daily, for it would be contrary to John, who interposes eight days in which he was not seen by them, that he might be made manifest the third time, and for as many days he fasted before his death, being in need of food, whereas he ate after the resurrection being now not in need of food. He fasted before his death, that we might abstain from the desires of this world. He ate, teaching by this that he is with us until the consummation of the world. Fasting is in the contest, because he who is in the struggle abstains from all things. Food is in the hope of peace, which shall be perfect, when this mortal shall have put on immortality. But we, while we take the way of the Lord, fast from the vanity of the world, and are refreshed by the promise to come.

((RAB.)) Through forty days, not continually, but at certain turns taken within that quadragenary number of days.

*And we drank. ((BEDA.))* Here Peter sets forth what is passed over in silence in the Gospel, that after the resurrection he drank with Christ, unless perhaps we believe it to be indicated there, where he says: *Until I drink it with you in the kingdom of my Father ((Matth. XXVI))*.

*Let him now say.* ((ID.)) As I admonish you, so do you admonish one another; or, *let him say,* that is, let him confess.

*Because for ever.* Behold four verses of one ending.

notes.text: If in this life only we have hope — If we look for nothing beyond the grave. But if we have a divine evidence of things not seen, if we have "a hope full of immortality," if we now taste of "the powers of the world to come," and see "the crown that fadeth not away," then, notwithstanding" all our present trials, we are more happy than all men.

But now — St. Paul declares that Christians "have hope," not "in this life only." His proof of the resurrection lies in a narrow compass, ver. 12-19. Almost all the rest of the chapter is taken up in illustrating, vindicating, and applying it. The proof is short, but solid and convincing, that which arose from Christ's resurrection. Now this not only proved a resurrection possible, but, as it proved him to be a divine teacher, proved the certainty of a general resurrection, which he so expressly taught. The first fruit of them that slept - The earnest, pledge, and insurance of their resurrection who slept in him: even of all the righteous. It is of the resurrection of these, and these only, that the apostle speaks throughout the chapter.

As through Adam all, even the righteous, die, so through Christ all these shall be made alive — He does not say, "shall revive," (as naturally as they die,) but shall be made alive, by a power not their own.
Afterward — The whole harvest. At the same time the wicked shall rise also. But they are not here taken into the account.

Then — After the resurrection and the general judgment. Cometh the end - Of the world; the grand period of all those wonderful scenes that have appeared for so many succeeding generations. When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to the Father, and he (the Father) shall have abolished all adverse rule, authority, and power - Not that the Father will then begin to reign without the Son, nor will the Son then cease to reign. For the divine reign both of the Father and Son is from everlasting to everlasting. But this is spoken of the Son's mediatorial kingdom, which will then be delivered up, and of the immediate kingdom or reign of the Father, which will then commence. Till then the Son transacts the business which the Father hath given him, for those who are his, and by them as well as by the angels, with the Father, and against their enemies. So far as the Father gave the kingdom to the Son, the Son shall deliver it up to the Father, John xiii, 3. Nor does the Father cease to reign, when he gives it to the Son; neither the Son, when he delivers it to the Father: but the glory which he had before the world began, John xvii, 5; Heb. i, 8, will remain even after this is delivered up. Nor will he cease to be a king even in his human nature, Luke i, 33. If the citizens of the new Jerusalem" shall reign for ever," Rev. xxii, 5, how much more shall he?
He must reign — Because so it is written. Till he - the Father hath put all his enemies under his feet. Psalm cx, 1.

The last enemy that is destroyed is death — Namely, after Satan, Heb. ii, 14, and sin, ver. 56, are destroyed. In the same order they prevailed. Satan brought in sin, and sin brought forth death. And Christ, when he of old engaged with these enemies, first conquered Satan, then sin, in his death; and, lastly, death, in his resurrection. In the same order he delivers all the faithful from them, yea, and destroys these enemies themselves. Death he so destroys that it shall be no more; sin and Satan, so that they shall no more hurt his people.

glossa.text: *For by a man indeed.* Behold the first-fruits, man and man, a man unto life, a man unto death, but that one is nothing other than man, this one is God and man.
*And as.* By *as,* a likeness and a cause are noted, because as from the corruption of Adam unto death, so from the Spirit of Christ unto life.

*Every one.* He sets forth the orders, as of a thing certain: and the times, when it was done, and when it shall be, that the dead may rise again. *Then they who are.* Another reading: *Then these who are Christ's, at his coming,* namely, shall rise again. And so those who believe in Christ, and are less worthy than he, shall rise later in time, and lesser in dignity. And who they are that are Christ's, he sets forth by adding: *Who have believed at his coming,* etc.

*Then the end.* This he sets down for the commendation of the resurrection, which being fulfilled there will be the end of the world and the consummation of all things. *When he shall have brought to nought.* While the world lasts, angels are set over angels, demons over demons, men over men: unto the profit of the living, or unto their deception. But when men have been gathered in, among angels and men every prelacy will cease, there will not be that dissension between those who preside and those who are subject. But then it will be known to all that none of these things did any earthly or heavenly beings possess of themselves, but from him from whom are all things.

*But he must reign.* The sense is: His kingdom must meanwhile be made manifest, until all his enemies confess that he reigns: by saying *until* he excludes a greater manifestation, not a longer continuance of the kingdom. Whence elsewhere: *Our eyes are unto the Lord our God, until he have mercy,* etc. Not that they are then turned away, but that they seek nothing further.

*But the last.* Among other things it is plain that Christ has also the power of raising up, when he adds: *But last of all the enemy death shall be destroyed.* Now Christ reigns, and then he shall reign: but last of all, that is, after all things, death shall be destroyed, because men shall no more be dissolved, as the heretics judge. *Last of all.* Because there will not be anything which it may destroy; after this mortal shall have put on immortality. *The enemy.* To whom we are enemies: or it to us. Again a commendation of the resurrection.

notes.text: Matt. xxviii, 1; Mark xvi, 1; Luke xxiv, 1.
Peter went out — Of the city.
Peter seeth the linen clothes lie — and the napkin folded up - The angels who ministered to him when he rose, undoubtedly folded up the napkin and linen clothes.
He saw — That the body was not there, and believed - That they had taken it away as Mary said.
For as yet — They had no thought of his rising again.
They went home — Not seeing what they could do farther.
But Mary stood — With more constancy. Mark xvi, 9.
Jesus saith to her, Mary — With his usual voice and accent.

Touch me not — Or rather, Do not cling to me (for she held him by the feet,) Matt. xxviii, 9. Detain me not now. You will have other opportunities of conversing with me. For I am not ascended to my Father - I have not yet left the world. But go immediately to my brethren -- thus does he intimate in the strongest manner the forgiveness of their fault, even without ever mentioning it. These exquisite touches, which everywhere abound in the evangelical writings, show how perfectly Christ knew our frame. I ascend - He anticipates it in his thoughts, and so speaks of it as a thing already present. To my Father and your Father, to my God and your God - This uncommon expression shows that the only- begotten Son has all kind of fellowship with God. And a fellowship with God the Father, some way resembling his own, he bestows upon his brethren. Yet he does not say, Our God: for no creature can be raised to an equality with him: but my God and your God: intimating that the Father is his in a singular and incommunicable manner; and ours through him, in such a kind as a creature is capable of.

glossa.text: *And they ran.* John signifies the Synagogue, which came first to the tomb but did not enter, because she heard the prophecies concerning the incarnation and the passion, but refused to believe him even dead. Peter signifies the Church, which knew him dead in the flesh and believed him living God; after whom she too, in Judaea, will enter at the end.

*It is separated.* Because the sacraments of the Godhead are incomprehensible and set far from the knowledge of our weakness. In a thing wrapped up, neither end nor beginning is seen. So the loftiness of the Godhead neither began to be, nor ceases. *Into one place.* Because God is not in the sundering of minds, but in unity. Or, the napkin of the head is the passion of Christ, whose sacraments are hidden apart from unbelievers, because it is far from ours, because he suffered willingly and without fault, we unwillingly and with fault.
*For as yet.* That is, to such a degree that, although it was openly said by the Lord himself, because of their custom of hearing parables from him, they did not understand.

*Weeping.* She now weeps more for him taken away than for him slain, because of so great a master, whose life had been taken from her, not even the memory remained, and this grief held her there. *While therefore,* etc. Although she knew that he was not there, yet because she grieves too much, she gave no thought either to her own eyes or to the eyes of those two who believed. Or rather this was done by divine prompting.

*She saw two.* The angels, that is, messengers, signify that the Gospel of Christ is to be announced from the head even to the feet, that is, from the beginning even to the end. And he was to be announced from his passion, because he is God before the ages, and man at the end of the age. The angel therefore sits at the head when he says: *In the beginning was the Word.* At the feet, when he says: *The Word was made flesh.* Or the two angels are the two Testaments, the one former, the other following. Joined together, while with equal sense they announce him incarnate, dead, raised again.

*Why weepest thou?* As if he should say: *Sin not* *peccare*; read *plorare*, "Do not weep" -- the next sentence says what is forbidden is her tears. They forbid her tears, in a manner announcing joy. But she, thinking that they asked as not knowing, brings forth the cause of her tears: *Because they have taken away my Lord,* that is, the body of my Lord.
*And she knew not that it was Jesus,* etc. Because she had her back toward him whom she believed not to have risen; because she loved and doubted, she saw and did not know him.

*Whom seekest thou? She, thinking that it was the gardener, saith to him.* Not that he doubted whom she was seeking, but because she knows not whom she seeks; for she seeks not Christ, but him whom she thinks carried off. *Lord.* Him whom she thinks a gardener she calls Lord, that she might honour the man of whom she was asking a kindness. Nor does she call him Lord in the same way as she calls him whom she seeks as taken away. But recognizing Jesus she calls him master, because she calls to mind him from whom she was learning to distinguish things human and divine. *If thou hast taken him away.* She does not say whom, because the force of love works this in the mind, that of him whom she always thinks she believes no other to be ignorant.

*Mary. She turning saith to him: Rabboni, which is to say master. Jesus saith to her.* After he had called her by the common name, and was not recognized, he calls her by her name, as if he should say, Know again him by whom thou art known again.

*Mary of Magdalene came announcing to the disciples that she had seen the Lord,* etc. There the fault is cut off *undet* it proceeded. A woman gave death to a man to drink; now a woman announces life to men; and she who then [told] the words of the serpent now relates the words of the Life-giver; as if God should say by the very facts: From what hand the draught of death was brought in, from that same hand receive ye the draught of life.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
While it was still dark, Mary came to the tomb and found the stone moved away.
She turned, and a known voice spoke her name.
This is the day the Lord has made;
the stone the builders rejected is now the cornerstone.
Go and tell it: we have seen the Lord.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come out into the garden while the dew is still on the grass and the sky is going from gray to gold.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
The tomb stands open and empty, the stone rolled back, the linen folded where the body had lain.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Mary stands there weeping, and a voice she knows says her name — Mary — and the morning breaks all the way open.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
This is the day the Lord has made; the gates of the righteous swing wide.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
So lift your heads and sing, all you who came here grieving:
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The garden is gray with dawn, the tomb thrown open.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
A known voice speaks her name, and grief turns to morning.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
This is the day the Lord has made.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us worship the living Lord.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
